\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 5 \\ -6 & 3 & -15 \\ 4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the matrix above has one pivot columns: the $1$st column. This tells us that $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{v}_1 \}$ forms a basis for our span.

![](images/10/104f03abf423695444fe4fdbdc9043aed6dbbfd7dc3388115a19a4d679f1ba74.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-6a087057-8a12-50fd-9bce-b13921276b0f" :question/id #uuid "6a087057-8a12-50fd-9bce-b13921276b0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-159782" :question/problem "Let ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ be linearly independent vectors, and suppose that the vector $w$ can be written as a linear combination of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ form a basis of $\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},w})=2$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}})=2$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a basis of a vector space $V$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that span $V.$ The dimension of $V$ is the number of vectors in any basis of $V$ (if such a basis exists). 

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, $\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is spanned by ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$, and we are told that ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ are linearly independent vectors. So, ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ is a basis of the span.

- Statement II is true. We are told that $w$ can be written as a linear combination of ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}.$ This means that $\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},w}$ is completely spanned by the vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ only. So, $\text{dim}(\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},w})=2.$

- Statement III is false. Indeed, $\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is spanned by ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$, and we are told that ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ are linearly independent vectors. So, ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ is a basis of the span. Therefore, we have $\text{dim}(\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}})=3$ (not $2$).

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bc8cd6e0-fec4-59f6-bf63-f95c9e73406a"] :db/ensure If the vector space $V$ has a basis with $n$ vectors, then any basis of $V$ has exactly $n$ vectors.

The number $n$ of vectors in any basis of $V$ is called the **dimension of the space** $V$ and is denoted $\textrm{dim}(V).$

For example, consider the linear span below:
![](images/3f/3f4139a1701c74e72ca55b662b1d5c06b02f1d3b6cab9a96b4667439dc196068.svg)

We know that, in order to find a basis of the span, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -6 \\ -1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the matrix above has two pivot columns: the $1$st and the $3$rd columns. This tells us that
$\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_3 \}$ is a basis of $H.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ consists of two vectors, *any basis* of $H$ will also have *exactly* two vectors. So, we have $\textrm{dim}(H)=2.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121057 :tutorial/content "We can build some geometric intuition for finite-dimensional vector spaces. To illustrate, let's find the dimensions of $\{\mathbf{0}\},$ $\mathbb{R},$ $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and $\mathbb{R}^3.$

First, note that $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ can be written as $\mathbb{R}^0,$ and $\mathbb{R}$ can be written as $\mathbb{R}^1.$ We have the following standard bases:

![](images/44/44f00659592bc6ac2742af0105fa493efa93e58e8dd63ee9af56a2d90b0e513a.svg)

Consequently, we have the following dimensions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{dim}({R}^{0})=0,\,\text{dim}({R}^{1})=1,\,\text{dim}({R}^{2})=2,\,\text{dim}({R}^{3})=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's build some geometric intuition. We can represent the standard bases in the following diagram:

![](images/16/169b5597d89fa32fd09772593cc2a9a330ee12881281dea4e3e43dc6165b9ebd.png)

So, the sequence $\mathbb{R}^0,$ $\mathbb{R}^1,$ $\mathbb{R}^2,$ $\mathbb{R}^3,$ $\ldots$ can be visualized as follows:

![](images/37/379823eca26d43337744a8f4a3872e67ac537a6c193d55e39b5d6761f258f6f5.png)

Notice the following:

- The basis for $\mathbb{R}^0$ is represented geometrically as a $0$-dimensional point.

- The basis for $\mathbb{R}^1$ is represented geometrically as a $1$-dimensional line segment.

- The basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$ is represented geometrically as a $2$-dimensional square.

- The basis for $\mathbb{R}^3$ is represented geometrically as a $3$-dimensional cube.

Unfortunately, we can't visualize dimensions greater than $3,$ but we know that $\mathbb{R}^n$ has the following standard basis consisting of $n$ vectors:

![](images/c8/c8a606f297f86b56224cb9f50ba68b826e614d4f075b396a4104e19bc77c46e7.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n) = n.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120056 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]
